meta.title: Make It Stick: The Science of Successful Learning
meta.author: Peter C. Brown, Henry L. Roediger III, Mark A. McDaniel
meta.publisher: The Belknap Press of Harvard University Press

parts.title: Make It Stick: The Science of Successful Learning - Introduction and Key Concepts
parts.body: This book, "Make It Stick: The Science of Successful Learning," by Peter C. Brown, Henry L. Roediger III, and Mark A. McDaniel, argues that common learning methods are often ineffective. Based on 125 years of research, the authors present evidence-based strategies that are counterintuitive but highly effective. They explain how learning and memory work through stories of mastery, rather than just reciting research. The book emphasizes that learning is deeper when effortful, and retrieval practice (recalling information) is more effective than rereading. Spaced repetition and interleaving different topics improve retention. They also debunk the idea of learning styles, advocating for a "go wide" approach using all aptitudes. The authors stress the importance of identifying underlying principles through interleaved and varied practice, and using testing as a tool to pinpoint weaknesses. Prior knowledge is crucial, and elaboration (connecting new information to existing knowledge) helps overcome the illusion of a "full brain." The book concludes by highlighting that intellectual ability is not fixed; every time you learn, you change your brain, and mistakes are essential for advanced learning.

parts.title: Effective Learning vs. Illusions of Knowing
parts.body: The text highlights ineffective study methods like rereading and repetition, which create an illusion of mastery. Studies show that repeated exposure or rereading in close succession doesn't lead to durable learning or better recall on delayed tests. For example, people often fail to identify a common penny correctly despite seeing it many times, or a fire extinguisher near their office, demonstrating that mere repetition doesn't embed information in memory. College students often rely on highlighting and rereading, leading to poor metacognition—they overestimate what they know and don't recognize their weaknesses. In contrast, active retrieval or testing is presented as a powerful learning tool. It strengthens memory, helps identify knowledge gaps, and reconsolidates memories, making future recall easier. The example of neurosurgeon Mike Ebersold demonstrates how reflection and repeated retrieval practice turn complex procedures into reflexive actions, essential for high-stakes situations. The text argues against the false dichotomy of knowledge vs. creativity, asserting that strong knowledge is the foundation for higher-level skills and nuanced creativity. Testing, when viewed as retrieval practice rather than just measurement, is crucial for interrupting forgetting and achieving durable learning.

parts.title: The Testing Effect: A Historical Overview of Laboratory Research
parts.body: The testing effect, first studied in 1917, shows that reciting material from memory leads to better retention than simply rereading it. Children who spent about 60% of their study time reciting showed the best results. A 1939 study with over three thousand sixth graders found that forgetting nearly stopped once a student took a test, and longer delays before the first test led to greater forgetting. However, interest in testing as a learning tool declined around 1940, shifting focus to forgetting. Interest in the testing effect resurfaced in 1967, with studies showing that repeated testing is as effective as repeated studying for learning. In 1978, research found that cramming (massed studying) leads to faster forgetting compared to practicing retrieval. Multiple tests significantly boost long-term retention, especially when spaced out. Even small efforts like filling in missing letters (generation effect) strengthen memory. Delaying retrieval practice can be more effective than immediate practice, as it requires more effort. The schedule of testing matters, with spaced retrieval practice leading to stronger long-term retention than massed practice.

parts.title: Interleaving and Varied Practice: The Path to Deeper Learning
parts.body: This text discusses why interleaving (mixing up different topics or skills during practice) and varied practice are more effective for long-term retention and mastery, even though they can feel sluggish or confusing at first. Teachers and students often dislike interleaving because it doesn't show immediate improvement, unlike massed practice (focusing on one topic intensely). However, research, including neuroimaging studies, shows that varied practice engages different parts of the brain and leads to a more flexible understanding that can be applied to new situations. It helps you develop discrimination skills to tell different problems apart. The text gives examples, like the beanbag study where varied practice led to better results, and athletes who historically used massed practice are slowly adopting varied training. It also highlights how these principles apply to cognitive learning, like solving anagrams or identifying bird species. Even when students experience better results from interleaving, they often prefer massed practice, showing how deeply ingrained the myths of massed practice are. Ultimately, interleaving and variation are crucial for moving beyond simple memorization to higher levels of conceptual learning and complex mastery.

parts.title: How Learning Occurs: Encoding, Consolidation, and Retrieval
parts.body: Learning involves three key stages: encoding, consolidation, and retrieval. Encoding is how your brain turns sensory information into memory traces, like temporary notes. While some information is short-term and soon forgotten, crucial learning needs to be stronger and more durable. Consolidation is the process of strengthening these memory traces for long-term memory. It's like refining a rough draft – the brain reorganizes and stabilizes memories, making connections to existing knowledge. This process takes time and is aided by things like sleep. Retrieval, especially after a lapse of time (reconsolidation), also strengthens memories, making them easier to access later. Trying to recall information, even if difficult, improves long-term retention.

parts.title: The Power of Generative Learning and the Importance of Failure
parts.body: Learning is a three-step process: encoding into short-term memory, consolidation into long-term memory (which reorganizes and stabilizes memories, gives them meaning, and connects them to prior knowledge), and retrieval, which updates learning and allows for application. Learning always builds on existing knowledge, and long-term memory is virtually limitless; more knowledge means more connections for new information. The ability to locate and recall information is crucial, depending on repeated use (to strengthen retrieval routes) and powerful retrieval cues. Effortful retrieval, especially when learning is a bit rusty, strengthens memory and makes it pliable for reconsolidation, updating and connecting to newer learning. Repeated effortful recall helps integrate learning into mental models, allowing for adaptable application. Varied practice and interleaving improve discrimination, induction, and versatility. Trying to generate an answer or solve a problem before being shown the solution (generative learning), even if incorrect but followed by corrective feedback, leads to better learning and retention than passive reception. The text then transitions to the next chapter's topic: avoiding illusions of knowing.

parts.title: Illusions and Memory Distortions
parts.body: Our memory is constantly being shaped by a hunger for narrative and a desire to resolve ambiguity. This means we often try to create a cohesive story out of events, even inconsequential ones. A study showed that overhearing one side of a phone conversation was more distracting and better recalled because people tried to infer the missing parts to form a complete narrative. This need for a rational understanding extends to our own lives, where we fit events into a story that explains our circumstances and choices. Narrative and memory become one, influencing how we make sense of new experiences and shaping our memories to fit existing constructs. People often rely on personal narratives to explain their emotions, even when reading online articles, and are surprisingly insensitive to the uniqueness of their own perceptions. While memory's changeable nature can skew perceptions, it's also essential for learning. Each time we recall a memory, the neural pathways strengthen, allowing us to deepen learning and broaden connections. Memory is like a Google search algorithm: the more you connect new information to what you already know and make associations, the easier it is to retrieve later. However, because memory is a shape-shifter influenced by emotion, suggestions, and narrative, our certainties can be fallible, and even cherished memories may not be entirely accurate. Memory is a reconstruction, filling gaps with details consistent with our narrative but not always correct. This can lead to remembering implied but unstated things (like the Helen Keller example) and imagination inflation, where vividly imagining an event makes us believe it actually happened. Suggestion can also distort memory, as seen in the car collision study where wording influenced speed estimates. The act of guessing about possible events can lead to creating misinformation, which is why hypnotically-induced testimony is often inadmissible. Interference from other events can also distort memory, as shown by the Donald Thomson case where a witness confused a TV personality with an assailant.

parts.title: Effective Learning: Beyond Preferences to Practical Skills
parts.body: This chapter acknowledges learning preferences but argues that aligning instruction with these preferences doesn't necessarily lead to better learning. Instead, it focuses on other significant differences in how people learn, introducing the story of Bruce Hendry to illustrate these points. Bruce's early life shows his proactive learning style and his ability to take charge of his own education. From selling string and fireworks to buying real estate and managing properties, he consistently learned from his experiences. The text highlights his ability to extract underlying principles (rule learning) and construct mental models (structure building) from new information, which are presented as crucial learning differences. He learned to identify key information and disregard irrelevant details, even if it meant facing setbacks, as seen in his early real estate and stock market ventures. His later success in distressed assets, like bonds in bankrupt companies and railroad equipment, stemmed from his deep dive into details, understanding complex structures, and challenging existing power dynamics.

parts.title: Rule versus Example Learning
parts.body: When learning, some people are "rule learners" who focus on abstracting principles, while others are "example learners" who tend to memorize specific examples. Rule learners can apply underlying rules to new situations, but example learners struggle without a grasp of the rules, often generalizing from irrelevant examples. However, example learners can improve by comparing two different examples to identify similarities and underlying principles. For instance, problems like a general attacking a castle or destroying a tumor both require dividing a large force into smaller ones to converge on a target without adverse outcomes. Identifying these commonalities helps students solve other "convergence problems." Like "high structure-builders", rule learners are more successful at transferring knowledge to unfamiliar situations. There's a potential link between being a high structure-builder and a rule learner, though more research is needed. This development of structure-building and rule-learning skills is seen in children learning jokes; a three-year-old may miss the joke's structure, but a five-year-old understands the "rule" that a punchline needs a setup. Bruce Hendry's experience with fireworks and boxcars illustrates how an initial understanding of supply and demand evolves into more complex "knowhow" by integrating various knowledge blocks into a larger structure. Knowhow isn't just knowledge; it's understanding underlying principles and fitting them together to enable action.

parts.title: The Impact of Praise and Growth Mindset
parts.body: This text discusses the power of praise and how it influences how people approach challenges, drawing on Dweck's research. In one study, fifth graders were praised for either being smart or for working hard after solving a puzzle. The majority of those praised for being smart chose an easier next puzzle, while 90% of those praised for effort chose a harder one, showing that emphasizing effort leads to embracing challenges. The text also explores how praise for intelligence can lead to helplessness when faced with failure, as seen in a study where "smart" praised students struggled with previously solved puzzles when they believed they were unsolvable. It highlights that success relies more on grit, curiosity, and persistence than on IQ. The key takeaway from Dweck and others is that a growth mindset, discipline, and grit are crucial for higher learning and success, emphasizing that the power to increase your abilities is largely within your own control.

parts.title: Effective Learning Strategies: Generation, Reflection, Calibration, and Mnemonics
parts.body: This text discusses various learning strategies and provides real-world examples of how they are applied by students and professionals. Generation involves trying to answer questions or solve problems *before* being given the answers. This makes the mind more receptive to new learning. For instance, filling in missing words in a text or engaging in experiential learning (learning by doing) are forms of generation. You can practice this by trying to explain key ideas in new material *before* reading it, which makes you more astute at gleaning substance. Solving problems before class in subjects like science or math also falls under generation, and while some students resist, professors find it strengthens classroom learning. Reflection is a combination of retrieval practice and elaboration, adding depth to learning. It involves reviewing recent learning, asking what went well, what could be better, and how it connects to other knowledge. Calibration is about aligning your judgment of what you know with objective feedback to avoid the "illusions of mastery." Quizzes and practice tests are crucial for this, and it's important to *actually answer* the questions, not just think you know them. Mnemonic devices are mental tools that help you store and retrieve arbitrary information, like using an acronym to remember a list. These strategies are not just for students; the text shows how actors like Nathaniel Fuller use them to learn roles and how writer John McPhee uses "awful blurting" (a form of generation) to overcome writer's block. Even a pianist like Thelma Hunter uses elaboration, visualizing scores and making mental notes, to deepen her learning.

parts.title: Effective Learning Strategies and High-Structure Teaching
parts.body: Mary Pat Wenderoth, a physiology professor, uses dense cartoon summaries with callouts, blowups, and directional arrows to help students synthesize weekly information and understand how systems are connected (e.g., “This is causing this, which causes this, which feeds back on those.”). She encourages collaboration but requires individual submission. Occasionally, she assigns low-stakes “learning paragraphs” to stimulate retrieval and reflection, asking questions like “How is the GI tract like the respiratory system?” or “What would you do differently next time?” These exercises prevent procrastination and help science majors practice clear prose writing. Wenderoth also translates Bloom’s taxonomy into her test answer keys, providing different answers for knowledge, understanding, and analysis levels, so students can identify their learning level and strive for higher understanding. She and her colleagues have found that high-structure classes (daily and weekly low-stakes exercises) significantly reduce student failure rates and narrow the achievement gap in gateway biology courses, while also improving exam results at higher Bloom’s taxonomy levels. They emphasize the importance of a “growth mindset”—that learning is hard work and struggle increases intellectual abilities—and show students how to persevere. Students in classes where exercises contribute to their grade, even minimally, show higher success. Wenderoth highlights that every discipline has a culture, and they teach students to “think like the professionals they want to become,” guiding them through setbacks. Michael D. Matthews, a psychology professor at West Point, utilizes the Thayer method, developed almost two centuries ago, which sets specific learning objectives and places responsibility on students. This method incorporates quizzing and recitation in every class. West Point cadets face immense academic, military, and physical demands, requiring them to prioritize essential information. Matthews tells students that reading every word of a chapter is inefficient; instead, they should start with questions and read for answers. His courses have little to no lecturing, beginning with a quiz on learning objectives. Students often “take to the boards,” collaborating on higher-order questions that require integrating and applying ideas, functioning as retrieval practice, generation, and peer instruction. One student from each group presents their solution, which is then critiqued. The focus is on constructs, not specific facts, and other exercises also aim at understanding and articulating broader concepts. Clear learning objectives, daily quizzing, and active problem-solving with feedback keep students engaged. A key skill taught is “shooting an azimuth”—keeping one’s bearings in unfamiliar territory—which Matthews likens to quizzing as a way to check mastery. Cadet Kiley Hunkler, a Rhodes Scholar, exemplified this by creating her own learning objectives for the MCAT and using practice tests every three days to identify weaknesses and adjust her study approach, focusing on understanding concepts rather than memorization. The Thayer method, including daily participation, is particularly effective for students who may not work hard independently, helping them develop effective learning habits in rigorous environments.

parts.title: Embrace Difficulties
parts.body: Chapter 4: Embrace Difficulties This chapter delves into the concept of desirable difficulties in learning, emphasizing that making learning tasks harder can lead to better retention and understanding. It introduces the three stages of memory: encoding, storage, and retrieval, and explains how issues at any stage can lead to forgetting or false memories. The chapter highlights the importance of retrieval cues and how forgetting can actually aid new learning by prompting more effortful reconsolidation. It also discusses the benefits of interleaving and generation effects, where active engagement with the material, like solving problems or creating explanations, significantly improves learning. Further, the chapter challenges the idea of errorless learning, arguing that making and correcting errors is crucial for robust learning, especially when paired with feedback. It explores how difficulties, such as those presented by interfering information or disfluent text, can enhance comprehension and memory. The role of reconsolidation in strengthening and updating memories after retrieval is also covered. The chapter concludes by reinforcing the idea that active, effortful engagement with challenging material, rather than passive reception, is key to truly embedding knowledge and skills.
